title: Even Out Two Fruit Baskets
statement:
Two baskets hold the same number of fruits. basket1[i] and basket2[i] are the prices of the fruits in them.

You may swap any fruit from the first basket with any fruit from the second, as many times as you like. A swap of fruits priced x and y costs min(x, y).

The goal is that both baskets hold exactly the same prices, in any order. Return the lowest total cost to get there, or -1 if it cannot be done.

examples.why: Each basket should hold 1, 3, 4. Swap a 1 from the first basket with a 4 from the second: cost min(1, 4) = 1.
Swapping 20 with 30 directly costs 20. Instead use the cheap 1 as a go-between: swap the first basket's 1 with a 30 (cost 1), then a 20 with the 1 now in the second basket (cost 1).
There are three 3s in total. An odd count can never be split evenly between two baskets.

hints: First decide if it is possible at all. What must be true of the total count of each price across both baskets?

Count, per price, how many extra copies the first basket has compared to the second. Half of each surplus has to move. Those moved fruits are paired one from each side, and a swap costs the cheaper of the pair.

Sort the fruits that must move. The cheapest half pays for every swap. But a fruit priced x can also be moved with two swaps through the cheapest fruit overall, costing 2 · low. Each swap costs min(x, 2 · low).

explain.intuition:
If a price appears an odd number of times in total, the baskets can never match: return -1. Otherwise each basket must end with exactly half of every price. Compare counts per price: where the first basket has a surplus of d copies, d / 2 of them must leave, and the same on the other side. The fruits that must move form a list with as many from each basket.

Each direct swap moves one fruit each way and costs the cheaper of the two. Sort the list of movers: pairing the cheapest half with the most expensive half makes the cheap ones pay every time. Now the trick: the cheapest fruit in either basket, low, can act as a go-between. Two swaps through it move any pair for 2 · low, and the go-between ends up back in a basket with the same counts. So each pair costs min(x, 2 · low), where x is the cheaper fruit of the pair.
steps: Compute diff[price] = count in basket1 − count in basket2, and low, the smallest price in either basket.
Build moves: each price repeated |diff| / 2 times. Sort it.
Add min(moves[i], 2 · low) for the first half of moves, and return the sum.
pitfalls: Missing the go-between move. In the second example direct swaps cost 20, but routing through the 1 costs 2.
Checking only that each basket can be sorted, or only that the totals are equal. The count of every price must be even.
Paying for all movers instead of only the cheaper half. Each swap moves two fruits, one each way, for one price.

solutions.title: Shortest path over basket states
solutions.idea: Treat each possible content of the first basket as a node and each swap as an edge with its cost. Dijkstra finds the cheapest way to the balanced state. Only usable for tiny baskets.

solutions.title: Count surpluses, pay with the cheap half
solutions.idea: Half of every surplus must move. Sort the movers; the cheaper half pays for the swaps, each at most twice the cheapest fruit overall.

followups: Why is the go-between always the single cheapest fruit, and why is one detour through it never improved by a longer chain?
Avoid the full sort: which selection algorithm gives the cheaper half in linear time?
